claims.text: Explicitly incorporating oxygen-induced defects and local compositional inhomogeneities will improve conductivity-prediction accuracy for HfNbTaTiZr relative to defect-free analytical models.
One wt.% oxygen acts as scattering centers that alter carrier mobility.
One wt.% oxygen alters phonon interactions differently in the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
As-cast bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing about 1 wt.% oxygen is a chemically disordered, single-phase BCC material.
The oxygen defects are distributed within the alloy.
Low-energy excitations and static disorder dominate conductivity behavior from 0 to 200 K.
Thermal phonon scattering is significant from 300 to 1200 K.
The presence and spatial distribution of oxygen modify the local electronic structure.
The presence and spatial distribution of oxygen modify phonon-scattering rates.
From 0 to 200 K, oxygen defects disrupt electronic coherence and increase electron scattering.
Increased low-temperature electron scattering reduces electrical conductivity relative to perfect-crystal predictions.
From 300 to 1200 K, oxygen defects enhance localized vibrational modes.
From 300 to 1200 K, oxygen defects alter phonon mean free paths.
A defect-inclusive model can capture oxygen-related high-temperature activation behavior more accurately than analytical models that neglect defects.
The defect-inclusive method will predict notably lower electrical conductivity from 0 to 200 K than perfect-crystal analytical models.
The defect-inclusive method will predict a smoother and more gradual conductivity temperature dependence from 300 to 1200 K.
The defect-inclusive method will reduce error against experimental conductivity data by more than about 10–15% relative to traditional predictions.
Traditional defect-free analytical approaches systematically overestimate conductivity in both temperature regimes when oxygen is present.
The proposed approach is applicable to HfNbTaTiZr containing around 1 wt.% oxygen over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The quantitative effect of oxygen on scattering varies with defect clustering and microstructural evolution.
